newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AMLC Beef Weekly - Australian export prices.
newsitem.headline: AMLC Beef Weekly - Australian export prices.

text.p: Australian Meat and Livestock Corp's (AMLC) weekly export prices are as follows:

AMLC COMMENTARY: In world beef markets this week, prices for Australian product, when denominated in US dollars, were firm to slightly higher in Japan but eased a little in the U.S. The depreciation of the A$ has enhanced export returns from the U.S. at similar level to last week.
The tone in Japanese wholesale markets has been much improved over the past fortnight. With this, and the upcoming Obon holiday less than a month away, the import market has also been on the rise.
Demand for items suited for yakiniku BBQ dishes have continued to improve, leading to a 25Y/kg and 45Y/kg lift in the price of cube rolls and tenderloins, respectively, on the Kanto wholesale market.

The other good news from Asia was the announcement of another South Korean tender. The tender, for 8,428 tonnes, comprises 648 tonnes of grassfed fullsets, 4000 tonnes of grassfed quarters and 400 tonnes of grainfed quarters, with grainfed cuts making up the remainder. The tender will be awarded next Tuesday, July 22. Product under this tender has to be shipped by the end of August.

In the U.S. this week, domestic lean beef prices came back but fatty trimmings prices increased. The weakness in the lean end is thought to have stemmed from a tightening in pasture conditions in some areas of the U.S., which has led to increased cow slaughter and lean beef supplies over the past week.

On the other side of the coin, fatty trimmings were supported by strength in U.S. cattle prices and futures market which improved 1-2USc/lb this week. These prices rose after spot market buying by some end-users, caught short of inventory, drove boxed beef prices higher.
There exists a large divergence of views about the future direction of cattle prices in the U.S. market at the present time.

Many analysts are expecting cattle prices to reach year lows in the next month. These thoughts are based on large cattle on feed inventories and a marketing rate that has been insufficient to keep feedlots current. They point to the sharp rise in carcase weights as being confirmation that this trend exists.

However, judging by activity in the futures market there are many market participants who are at odds with this assessment. August live cattle futures hit a three year contract high during mid-week and closed on Thursday (US time) at 66.5USc/lb.
Tonight's U.S. cattle on feed report will add another piece to the puzzle. Most analysts are expecting cattle on feed numbers to be 16 percent above last year.

In the Australian domestic market, April slaughter figures have been revised upwards quite sharply and the May kill has also proven extremely large. This, combined with large throughputs in New South Wales and Queensland during June-July
and record live cattle exports, has confirmed Australian cattle turnoff through the first half of 1997 as being the largest since the drought of 1982.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
